docs.title: Welcome to Stream-Ops 2.0
docs.text:
Stream-Ops is a research prototype for exploring speculative sandbox prewarming in tool-using LLM systems. Performance benefits have not yet been evaluated.

[ Streamed Ollama response text ] ──► [ Rust heuristic intent scorer ]
                                           └──► [ Go requests a Kubernetes pod ]

docs.title: The Core Problem: The Cold Start Dilemma
docs.text:
Creating a Kubernetes pod can add infrastructure delay. Its size depends on the cluster, image cache, scheduling conditions, and runtime; this repository has not established a general cold-start range.

Strategy Latency Impact Cloud Compute Cost Security & Isolation Always-On Static Pods ⚡ Instant (0s) 💸 Extremely Wasteful (Hundreds of idle pods) ⚠️ Risk of cross-tenant state leakage On-Demand Reactive Pods 🐢 5–15s Cold Penalty 💰 Minimal cost ✅ Fresh container per session Stream-Ops prototype Not evaluated Not evaluated Creates isolated-by-session named pods; isolation requires further review

docs.title: Key Highlights
docs.text:
• Rust scores ordinary Ollama response chunks using keywords and lexical similarity.
  • Go can create a real Kubernetes pod and delete expired unclaimed speculative pods.
  • The threshold uses static profile values; the score is not a calibrated probability.
  • The claim endpoint marks a pod claimed and waits for readiness; it does not execute tool code.
  • Performance, cost savings, multi-provider compatibility, and production isolation are not evaluated.

docs.title: Stream-Ops: A Prototype for Speculative Sandbox Prewarming in LLM Agent Systems
docs.text: Status: Prototype report; performance evaluation is not yet complete. Project: Stream-Ops, group K3C0047 Repository: https://github.com/yashrajshuklaaa/StreamOps2.0

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text:
Tool-using language-model agents can incur infrastructure delay when an execution environment is created only after a tool call. Stream-Ops explores whether a sandbox can be provisioned while an agent response is still streaming. The current prototype uses a Rust service to score streamed Ollama response text and a Go service to request a namespaced Kubernetes pod when a score passes a heuristic cost threshold. The services can be run locally in Kind.

This is an implementation report, not evidence of a latency improvement. The repository does not yet contain a reproducible agent-to-tool execution evaluation, a reactive baseline, or raw benchmark traces. The earlier speedup, cold-start masking, cloud-cost, and proxy-overhead figures are withdrawn. The prototype provisions an idle sandbox pod; it does not yet execute an agent's tool call inside that pod.

docs.title: 1. Scope and positioning
docs.text:
The hypothesis is that signals available before a formal tool invocation may provide time to start a sandbox concurrently with model generation. Whether a provider exposes useful reasoning signals is provider- and API-dependent. Stream-Ops currently inspects ordinary streamed Ollama response text; it does not establish access to private chain-of-thought or infer that generated text faithfully represents a later action.

Intent-aware sandbox prewarming is not new: SpecBox describes keyword and streaming-embedding intent detection, sandbox prewarming, and context-aware prefetching over a sandbox dependency graph [4]. Conveyor overlaps partial tool execution with decoding [2], Speculative Actions speculates on agent actions [3], and Continuum manages model KV-cache retention across agent tool calls [5]. These are related but distinct system mechanisms. This prototype does not claim to introduce intent-aware prewarming or to outperform these systems.

The limited contribution of the current artifact is an open, locally runnable Rust intent-scoring service connected to a Go Kubernetes pod lifecycle service, together with a testable Kind deployment. A cost-aware policy and rigorous comparison remain research goals, not established contributions.

docs.title: 2. Prototype implementation
docs.text:
The Rust service keeps bounded text state per stream session, applies keyword matching and a TF-IDF-style term-frequency/inverse-document-frequency similarity score, and evaluates the score against a threshold computed from static tool cost-profile values. These scores are heuristic; they are not calibrated probabilities. The current threshold uses configured constants, not live cloud prices or measured distributions.

The Go service proxies Ollama's newline-delimited generation response, sends each response chunk to the Rust service, and creates a namespaced Kubernetes pod when the service returns a trigger decision. It exposes a claim endpoint, pod readiness observation, TTL cleanup for unclaimed speculative pods, and Prometheus metrics.

The current implementation is a prototype, not a production Kubernetes operator. It supports the Ollama generation route only. The Python sandbox starts a sleeping process; the claim endpoint marks the pod as claimed and waits for readiness but does not execute code or accept an agent tool-call payload. There is no end-to-end agent integration, shared trace schema, provider adapter suite, OpenTelemetry instrumentation, preemptible priority class, or real tool execution yet.

docs.title: 3. Decision-policy status
docs.text:
The implementation's static threshold is a heuristic policy, not the lookahead-aware optimal-stopping policy proposed for future work. In particular, the detector's score is not a calibrated estimate of \(P(\text{tool }k\text{ is called}\mid\text{stream so far})\). The current cost profile uses hard-coded values and a fixed TTL, and does not model remaining reasoning time, an abort-time distribution, or the hidden portion of cold start.

Consequently, no optimality theorem or bounded-regret result is claimed here. Deriving and testing a race model, a lookahead-dependent decision rule, and hazard-rate or budget-aware cleanup policies are future work. The previous fixed-boundary derivation must not be interpreted as a proof for the deployed implementation.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation status
docs.text:
Performance evaluation: NOT EVALUATED.

There are no raw evaluation traces or result files under results/. The existing benchmarks/benchmark_suite.py computes TTFE and masking values from fixed token rates, cold-start constants, and a chosen trigger offset; its short sleeps do not measure those modeled durations. Its printed table is SIMULATED, not measured. benchmark_compare.py is also a timing demonstration based on fixed sleeps, not a benchmark of model inference or Kubernetes startup.

The earlier paper's numerical TTFE table, claimed 1.70x maximum speedup, 100% masking claim, 5–15-second general cold-start claim, cloud-cost savings, proxy-overhead measurements, and EKS/500-prompt/model evaluation description are withdrawn. They are unsupported by retained scripts and raw data and must not be cited as results. The local Kind smoke test demonstrated that a real Ollama stream can trigger creation of a real Kubernetes pod, but did not compare reactive and speculative end-to-end tool execution. It is not a latency experiment.

docs.title: Evaluation required before making performance claims
docs.text:
The next evaluation should pre-register workloads, model/provider versions, cluster configuration, policies, and metrics. It should retain raw per-run traces and report at least:

  • TTFE p50/p95/p99 for reactive and speculative execution;
  • measured cold-start and reasoning intervals, including their overlap;
  • prewarm precision, recall, hit rate, and wasted pod-seconds;
  • resource and cost measurements with the price source and date;
  • direct-inference proxy overhead and confidence intervals.

No sample count, improvement, cost saving, or confidence interval is reported until that evaluation has been run and its outputs are reproducible from versioned scripts and raw data.

docs.title: 5. Limitations and threats to validity
docs.text:
The current detector uses keyword and small-corpus lexical similarity, not a trained or calibrated intent model. Streamed response text can mention a tool without calling it, omit a later tool call, or be unrelated to an internal reasoning process. Research on chain-of-thought faithfulness cautions against treating visible explanations as reliable records of model reasoning [6]. Provider-specific stream fields and availability must be verified and evaluated separately; no general claim about access to private reasoning is made.

Kind smoke tests do not represent a production cluster's scheduler, image cache, network, contention, security boundary, or cloud pricing. Pod readiness is not equivalent to a working tool runtime, and claiming a pod is not tool execution. The prototype currently has no concurrent load study, reactive baseline, calibration analysis, statistical confidence intervals, or failure-injection evaluation.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: This reference describes the current Go control plane in services/control-plane/. It currently supports Ollama's /api/generate route; the legacy Python service has additional routes that are not part of this Go/Rust prototype.

docs.title: POST /api/generate
docs.text:
Forwards an Ollama generation request and streams the upstream NDJSON response. Each response chunk is also sent to the Rust intent service. When the intent service returns a trigger decision, the Go control plane creates a Kubernetes pod asynchronously.

The response includes an X-StreamOps-Session-ID header. Keep this value if you want to claim the corresponding speculative pod. A triggered pod is an idle sandbox; this endpoint does not execute generated code or tool calls.

docs.title: POST /v1/sessions/{session_id}/claim
docs.text:
Marks an existing speculative pod as claimed and waits for it to become ready. It does not run a tool payload.

Example:

POST /v1/sessions/0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef/claim
Content-Type: application/json

{"tool_name":"python"}

The response contains the pod name, namespace, readiness status, and timing fields. Timing returned by this endpoint is not an end-to-end TTFE measurement.

docs.title: GET /healthz and GET /readyz
docs.text: /healthz indicates that the Go process is running. /readyz checks the configured Kubernetes namespace API and Rust intent service.

docs.title: GET /metrics
docs.text:
Exposes Go process metrics and the following Stream-Ops counters/histograms:

  • streamops_intent_triggers_total
  • streamops_pod_create_errors_total
  • streamops_pod_trigger_to_ready_seconds
  • streamops_cold_start_seconds_masked_total
  • streamops_speculative_pods_reclaimed_total

The metric named streamops_cold_start_seconds_masked_total currently calculates the overlap of a recorded pod-ready time and a claim request. It does not establish an agent-generated tool call or an end-to-end latency benefit; interpret it as a prototype diagnostic only.

docs.title: System Architecture
docs.text:
This diagram describes the current local prototype, not a production operator or a measured high-throughput system.

flowchart TD
    Client([HTTP client]) -->|Ollama generate request| Go[Go control plane]
    Go -->|proxy request| Ollama[Ollama]
    Ollama -->|NDJSON response chunks| Go
    Go -->|chunk text, synchronous HTTP call| Rust[Rust intent service]
    Rust -->|heuristic decision| Go
    Go -->|create pod| K8s[Kubernetes API]
    K8s --> Pod[Idle speculative sandbox pod]
    Go -->|claim / TTL cleanup| K8s
    Go --> Metrics[Prometheus metrics endpoint]

docs.title: 1. Go Ollama proxy (services/control-plane/)
docs.text: Proxies Ollama's newline-delimited /api/generate route and inspects each response chunk. OpenAI and Anthropic adapters in the legacy Python tree are not used by this Go service. The prototype does not claim access to private reasoning.

docs.title: 2. Rust intent scorer (services/intent-engine/)
docs.text: Maintains a bounded per-session text buffer, performs keyword checks and TF-IDF-style lexical similarity, and compares a heuristic score against a threshold derived from static profile values. The score is not a calibrated probability. No per-token latency target has been measured.

docs.title: 3. Go Kubernetes lifecycle (services/control-plane/)
docs.text: Creates a named pod in a configured namespace, exposes a claim endpoint that marks it claimed and waits for readiness, and periodically deletes expired unclaimed pods. The sandbox process is idle; the claim endpoint does not execute a tool payload. Session-specific pod names and labels are not, by themselves, a security isolation guarantee.

docs.title: Not implemented or evaluated
docs.text: The current Go/Rust path is not a Kubernetes operator and has no CRDs, gRPC API, provider-adapter suite, lock-free side channel, OpenTelemetry spans, preemptible sandbox class, or end-to-end agent tool execution. Prometheus metrics are exposed, but a production observability stack and performance evaluation are not established by the prototype.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: The current prototype contains a Rust intent-scoring service and a Go Ollama-to-Kubernetes control plane. It is not yet a general multi-provider agent integration.

docs.title: Ollama stream inspection
docs.text: The Go proxy handles Ollama's newline-delimited /api/generate response and sends each response value to the Rust service. It does not currently normalize OpenAI, Anthropic, or DeepSeek streams, and it does not establish access to private chain-of-thought.

docs.title: Heuristic intent score
docs.text: The Rust service combines keyword matching and TF-IDF-style lexical similarity. It passes a heuristic score to a cost threshold derived from static tool-profile constants. The score is not calibrated as a probability, and a tool mention does not establish that the agent will execute that tool.

docs.title: Pod lifecycle
docs.text: The Go service creates a namespaced pod after a trigger, offers an endpoint to mark it claimed, observes readiness, and periodically deletes unclaimed pods after the configured TTL. Claiming is not tool execution. TTL cleanup does not guarantee zero resource leakage, and security/isolation properties have not been independently evaluated.

docs.title: Local Kind prototype
docs.text:
The Go control plane and Rust intent service can be built and deployed to a local Kind cluster using:

./scripts/run-kind.sh

The script creates a streamops Kind cluster, builds and loads the two service images, then deploys the services and Ollama. The local cluster exposes the Go service on http://localhost:8000. The repository README has a streaming smoke-test request.

The setup uses real Kubernetes pods, but does not execute tool payloads or represent a production deployment. The Ollama model must be downloaded separately, and cluster behavior depends on local machine resources and image availability.

docs.title: Legacy deployment examples
docs.text:
deploy/docker-compose.yml, deploy/helm/stream-ops/, and deploy/terraform/ predate the Go/Rust prototype. They describe examples for the legacy Python stack and have not been validated as deployment artifacts for the current services. The Helm chart and Terraform files must not be treated as production-ready infrastructure without review and testing.

The Go/Rust prototype does not yet include a Kubernetes operator, CRD-based reconciliation, production RBAC policy, NetworkPolicy, priority/preemption configuration, or a production observability deployment.

docs.title: FinOps Threshold Prototype
docs.text:
Status: illustrative model, not validated cloud-cost optimization. The current Go/Rust prototype uses hard-coded profile values and uncalibrated intent scores. It does not retrieve live prices, estimate remaining reasoning time, or establish that a trigger minimizes operational cost.

The equation below is a simplified expected-loss example. It assumes that P_k is a calibrated probability and that the listed costs accurately represent the decision. Those assumptions do not hold for the current prototype, so its threshold is heuristic rather than a proven optimal policy.

docs.title: Mathematical Derivation
docs.text: Let tool \(k\) have: - \(C_{\text{waste}}(k) = \text{cost\_per\_second} \times \text{TTL}\): Cost incurred if the speculative pod is created and discarded. - \(C_{\text{cold}}(k) = T_{\text{cold}} \times \mu_{\text{SLA}}\): Penalty incurred if the system fails to pre-warm and the user waits. - \(P_k = P(\text{Tool } k \mid \tau_{1:t})\): A calibrated probability would be required. The current detector's score is not such a probability.

docs.title: Expected Loss Comparison
docs.text:
\[\mathbb{E}[\text{Loss} \mid \text{Speculate}] = (1 - P_k) \cdot C_{\text{waste}}(k)$$ $$\mathbb{E}[\text{Loss} \mid \text{Wait}] = P_k \cdot C_{\text{cold}}(k)\]

Under those simplifying assumptions, the decision boundary would be:

\[(1 - P_k) C_{\text{waste}}(k) \le P_k C_{\text{cold}}(k)\] \[\boxed{\theta^*(k) = \frac{C_{\text{waste}}(k)}{C_{\text{waste}}(k) + C_{\text{cold}}(k)}}\]

This equation omits the remaining reasoning window and the portion of cold-start time that could be hidden. It is not the lookahead-aware rule proposed for future work, nor an optimality result for the deployed implementation.

docs.title: Hard-coded prototype profiles
docs.text:
The following are source-code configuration values, not live provider prices or measured cold-start distributions. They are retained for prototype behavior and must not be used for a cloud budget or a performance claim.

Tool vCPU / RAM Cost / sec Cold Start (\(T_{\text{cold}}\)) Waste Cost (\(C_{\text{waste}}\)) Penalty (\(C_{\text{cold}}\)) Optimal \(\theta^*\) Python Sandbox 0.5 vCPU, 512MB $0.00005 5.5s $0.0030 $0.0275 0.15 (Eager) PostgreSQL DB 0.5 vCPU, 512MB $0.00008 6.0s $0.0048 $0.0300 0.15 (Eager) Chromium Browser 1.5 vCPU, 2GB $0.00020 8.0s $0.0120 $0.0400 0.23 (Moderate) Bash 0.25 vCPU, 256MB $0.00003 3.0s $0.0018 $0.0150 0.15 (clamped)

No GPU profile or dynamic price integration is implemented. No claim is made that this policy minimizes spend, bounds expenditure, or improves latency. Calibration, current pricing inputs, lookahead-aware utility, and evaluation remain open work.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide will help you set up and run the Stream-Ops proxy and the visual demonstration.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.9+
  • Kubernetes cluster (e.g., Minikube or Docker Desktop with Kubernetes enabled)
  • (Optional) Ollama running locally for the POC simulation

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
1. Clone the repository and navigate to the project directory: 

    git clone https://github.com/your-username/stream-ops.git
cd stream-ops

  2. Install the required Python dependencies: 

    pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: Running the Proxy
docs.text:
Stream-Ops acts as a transparent middleware. Start the FastAPI proxy server:

python stream_proxy.py
The proxy will run on http://localhost:8000.

docs.title: Running the End-to-End Demo
docs.text:
We have provided a simulation script that demonstrates how Stream-Ops detects intents and saves latency.

In a separate terminal, run: 

python dummy_ollama.py   # Starts a simulated LLM on port 11434
python agent_demo.py     # Runs the interactive benchmark

docs.title: Running the Tests
docs.text:
To verify that the proxy and Kubernetes provisioning logic are functioning correctly: 

pytest tests/

docs.title: Viewing Metrics
docs.text:
Stream-Ops exposes standard Prometheus metrics. While the proxy is running, you can view the metrics at: 

curl http://localhost:8000/metrics
